fixes.explanation: That's the reason the writer gives. The next day was a High Sabbath, so the Jews asked Pilate, the Roman governor, to have the legs broken and the bodies taken down. The text says the point was that the bodies would not remain on the cross during the Sabbath.

I get why that sounds like a reasonable guess. But the text never says anything about the soldiers' schedule. It says the Jews asked Pilate, the Roman governor, so that the bodies would not remain on the cross during the Sabbath. The Sabbath is the reason on the page.

I see why you stopped at one, because the verse is short and moves fast. But it says the soldiers broke the legs of the first man crucified with Jesus, and those of the other. That's both men, not one.
That's right, baker! John 19:32 says the soldiers broke the legs of the first man who had been crucified with Jesus, and those of the other. So both men got the same treatment.

You've got the no, and that part is right. But Pilate doesn't step in anywhere in this verse. The text says the soldiers came to Jesus and saw that He was already dead, and that's why they did not break His legs.

That's a fair guess, because the scene is rough and fast. But the text says the opposite. John 19:36 says these things happened “so that the Scripture would be fulfilled,” and then gives the words: “Not one of His bones will be broken.” The writer says outright that the Scripture is the reason these things happened.

I see why you'd expect a no. But John 19:38 says Pilate gave permission, so Joseph came and removed the body. Joseph asked, and he got a yes. After all that hiding, I think that's a good moment for him.
That's right, baker. Joseph of Arimathea asked Pilate, and Pilate gave him permission. Then Joseph came and removed the body of Jesus. I bet asking took some nerve, but the answer was yes.
Nothing in the text has the spices going to the soldiers. It says Joseph and Nicodemus took the body of Jesus and wrapped it in linen cloths with the spices. The spices went with the burial cloths.

Lazarus is a good name to think of. Jesus called him “our friend” (John 11:11), and Jesus called him out of his tomb (John 11:43-44). But this garden has a different tomb, a new one in which no one had yet been laid. I think the writer wants us to notice that nobody had been in it.

That pool shows up earlier in John, in chapter 5 (John 5:2-9). But the garden here has something different. The text says there was a new tomb in which no one had yet been laid. That's a good memory, friend.
